Topic: Is a virtue still a virtue when practised only where the neighbours can see it?
Nietzsche — Judgement:
Every "virtue" that requires an audience is a herd-animal's bookkeeping — a coin minted for others' eyes, not a value coined from within.

Morality of this kind is slave morality's finest costume: the meek call "good" whatever earns them safety in the herd's regard, and dress their fear of judgement as humility, charity, restraint. But the neighbour's gaze is not a moral faculty — it is a leash. The one who is virtuous only when watched has not overcome anything; he has merely calculated the price of appearing to. Real virtue — what I would call the virtue of the free spirit, of one who has become who he is — needs no witness, because it is not a transaction with the crowd but a discharge of one's own strength and taste, private as breathing.

A virtue performed for spectators is not virtue but vanity wearing virtue's mask.

*What the neighbours must see you do, you have not yet done — you have only advertised it.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
I hold that virtue unwitnessed and virtue performed differ as candlelight differs from fire; conscience needs no audience, for it is itself the tribunal. A character formed only for the neighbours' eyes is not character but reputation, a paper currency that trades at par only while confidence lasts and collapses the instant the crowd looks away. I have said that my country is the world, and my religion to do good — and doing good for spectators alone is not religion but theatre, a hollow imitation that dissolves the moment applause stops. The test of any principle is whether it holds in the dark, alone, at cost, with nothing to be gained but the keeping of it.

A virtue performed only for spectators is not virtue but vanity wearing virtue's coat.

*Character is what a man does when he has convinced himself no one is counting.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Virtue, in my accounting, is not a quality of the soul but a species of behaviour men agree to call good because it serves peace; and behaviour performed only under observation is not virtue but the *appearance* of covenant-keeping, purchased at the price of vigilance. Strip away the neighbours' eyes and you strip away the sovereign power that made the performance rational — for in the state of nature, before any common power to keep men in awe, there is no place for industry, justice, or virtue at all, only the perpetual calculation of advantage. A man who is just only when watched has not internalised the covenant; he has merely priced the cost of detection above the profit of transgression, and will re-enter the state of war the instant that price falls. So no: it is not virtue, it is prudence wearing virtue's mask, and it will fail you exactly when you most need it — in the dark, alone, unwatched, where the real test of covenant always falls.

*The virtue that needs an audience was never virtue — it was merely fear, well dressed.*
Keynes — Judgement:
Public spirit that dies the moment the shutters close is not virtue at all — it is merely well-dressed vanity, a purchase of reputation rather than a discharge of duty.

I have always insisted that the springs of action which move a decent society are mixed — self-interest, yes, but also that "purposiveness" by which men delight in building for the sake of building, in giving for the sake of giving, whether an audience is present or not. A generosity contingent on witnesses is not moral conduct but a transaction in social esteem, priced no differently than any other vanity purchase, and it will evaporate precisely when unseen sacrifice is most needed — in the slump, in the private ledger, in the vote cast where nobody checks. The state cannot be built on performances that vanish once the curtain falls.

A virtue that requires an audience was never a virtue — it was advertising.

*The night is when we discover whether a man's conscience was ever anything more than his neighbours' opinion of him worn as a coat.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
A virtue performed for an audience and abandoned in solitude is not virtue but vanity in a modest dress. I have written that a woman taught to please rather than to reason will practise chastity as decoration, charity as display — good only insofar as good is witnessed, which is to say, not good at all, but a transaction with public opinion. The neighbour's gaze is a poor substitute for conscience; it disciplines conduct while leaving the heart entirely unreformed, and the moment surveillance lifts, so does the pretence. What we call virtue must survive the empty room, or it was never virtue but manners — and manners crumble the instant they stop being profitable. A being of reason owes obedience to principle, not to the drawing-room's opinion of them.

Practised only for spectators, it is not virtue but performance, and performance answers to no one when the curtain falls.

*Virtue rehearsed for an audience is merely vice with better manners.*
Hume — Judgement:
Virtue paraded before an audience is not virtue but reputation's cheaper cousin, mistaken for the thing itself by the very mind that performs it.

I have always held that no quality of mind is esteemed as a virtue without regard to its usefulness — but usefulness to whom? The neighbour-watching actor has simply relocated the calculation: instead of "does this serve society," it becomes "does this serve my standing in society." Sympathy, which properly binds us to others' pain, gets redirected into a concern for others' opinions of us. The action's effects on the world remain identical; only the motive curdles, and motive is what separates a virtuous character from a vigilant one.

A disposition that requires spectators to sustain itself was never a settled sentiment of the heart, only a performance rented by the hour.

*The virtue that vanishes when the room empties was never furniture of the soul, only scenery on its stage.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Virtue displayed only for an audience is not virtue at all — it is vanity wearing virtue's coat, and the impartial spectator I ask each of us to consult is not the neighbour peering over the fence but a judge seated in our own breast.

The neighbours' eyes train us in youth, and there is no shame in that; the "man without" first teaches the "man within" his lesson. But the merchant who is honest only when watched, the friend who is loyal only when it is seen, has not internalised the rule — he has merely calculated an audience. Real virtue survives the empty room; it is self-command exercised because propriety demands it, not because applause follows.

Practised only for spectators, it is not virtue but vanity's counterfeit, and it will desert you the instant the neighbours look away.

*He who is honest only before witnesses has made a covenant with his neighbours, but none with himself.*
